topics.title: [grug] Require NVIDIA before the SM100 check in ragged all-to-all
topics.body:
The ragged all-to-all MoE backend checks for an SM100 GPU before choosing the QuACK grouped-GEMM expert MLP, and parsed the device's `compute_capability` as a float. ROCm devices report an architecture name such as `gfx942`, so every expert-parallel run with `--moe-impl ragged_all_to_all` on AMD failed with `ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'gfx942'` while tracing the first step. The check now requires an NVIDIA device before it reads the compute capability, and other GPUs fall back to `ragged_dot`, as non-Blackwell NVIDIA GPUs already do.

The backend still does not run on ROCm. With this change, the June Snowball model on 8× MI300X (JAX 0.11, ROCm 10) compiles and then fails in the first step with `UNIMPLEMENTED: Device communicator is not implementing`, which points to XLA's RCCL communicator lacking ragged all-to-all. The `ring` and `fixed_all_to_all` backends run on the same node.

Part of #9462.

topics.title: [grug] Compute the MoE routing-weight gradient on the expert side
topics.body:
With QuACK's expert MLP, the ragged all-to-all MoE takes its routing-weight gradient from the expert MLP's own backward, so the backward needs neither the expert outputs nor their return transport, and the hero saves the routed output instead of recomputing the expert down projection, the return all-to-all and the combine. The step shortens by 4.12% (13.541 to 13.005 s against #9832, over 26 scored steps). Peak HBM rises to 125.4 GiB of the 143.75 GiB pool.

The backend chooses the gradient together with its expert MLP kernel; `moe_mlp` takes no option for it. QuACK's expert MLP (SM100, SiLU, QuACK installed) takes the expert-side gradient for bfloat16 and float32 tokens, which is the hero's configuration. The portable `ragged_dot` expert MLP takes the exact gradient, <dout, y> over the kept expert outputs: it keeps y anyway, so the expert-side gradient would save it only the returned [TK, H] buffer and the return transport. QuACK with float16 tokens takes the exact gradient too. The expert-side gradient is zero at a zero weight, and zero or inexact wherever |w * dout| falls below the cotangent dtype's smallest normal number: 2^-126 in bfloat16 and float32, which only output cotangents near underflow reach, and 2^-14 in float16, which ordinary magnitudes reach. The hero's routing weights are positive renormalized sigmoids and its cotangents bfloat16. Forward, dx, dW13 and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; the routing-weight gradient differs at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp) at nonzero weights.

The gradient with respect to the combine weight w[t,k] is dS[t,k] = <dout[t], y[t,k]>, the only backward consumer of the expert down projection's output y. Since dy = w * dout and dh = dy W2^T, the same value is rowsum(dh * h) / w, built from tensors the expert MLP backward already holds. One custom VJP from dispatch to combine returns s = <h, dh> per expert row, sends it back with one [C, 1] f32 all-to-all per chunk, and forms dS = s / w in f32; dropped and padded slots get 0 by selection. The backward's transports reuse the forward transfers' offsets, swapped, and on GPU its weighted output cotangents come from #9832's scatter kernel.

The saved routed output fits the 114 GiB remat budget that #9831 gives the carry offload; the backward needs ~105 GiB. With the backward's transports no longer ordered after the recompute's, several collectives in flight gave run-to-run different gradients or hung on GB200, so every ragged run forces a collective overlap limit of 1.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0), each head compiled fresh.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [grug] Prepare the hero handoff to the MoE optimization stack
topics.body:
Point the next hero launch at a new run, `hero-mfu30-step<N/1000>k`, that runs main with the MoE optimization stack (#9829–#9834) and continues `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k` from a checkpoint forced on it about 70 minutes before cutover. The run ID, the handoff checkpoint, and the W&B fork point are `REPLACE_BEFORE_DEPLOYMENT` placeholders until that checkpoint exists; `trigger_hero.sh` refuses to fork or launch while any placeholder remains.

On one GB200 NVL72 rack restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint, the stack trains 4K sequences at 12.70 s/step against 13.97 s/step before it (30.9% against 28.1% MFU), with peak HBM 124.0 GiB against an allocator limit of 143.8 GiB. The 8K and 16K speedups are +10.0% and +9.6% with unchanged expert-drop fractions. Single-rack runs do not exercise the 11-rack collectives, so the 200-step paired trial after cutover is the first multi-rack test.

Remaining steps, in order:

1. Merge #9958, which removes the launch's memory overrides; without it the launch aborts in compilation.
2. Confirm the d768 validation `validate9885-d768-20261008` passes ([report](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/x--VmlldzoxODA3OTE2Mg==)).
3. Force a checkpoint on `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k` through its training-control endpoint about 70 minutes before cutover. When its `metadata.json` exists, rewrite it with `is_temporary: false`, then copy it to the durable prefix in `HANDOFF_CHECKPOINT`.
4. Replace the placeholders with the forced step N, in one commit: the checkpoint path, the W&B `_step` of the parent row that records `global_step=N-1`, and the run ID `hero-mfu30-step<N/1000>k`.
5. Merge this PR. From a pristine checkout of the merged main, run `trigger_hero.sh fork-wandb`.
6. When the old run is 200 steps past N, cancel its coordinator, confirm that it is terminal, and run `trigger_hero.sh launch`.

topics.title: [levanter] Replace the Pallas short convolution with a Triton kernel
topics.body:
Short convolutions on GPU run in a new streaming Triton kernel that reads each tensor once, instead of once per tap. The Pallas kernel is deleted, and the package moves from `levanter.kernels.pallas.short_conv` to `levanter.kernels.triton.short_conv`. In a single-GPU hero block, short-convolution time per step falls from 4.45 to 1.76 ms.

| Shape | Direction | Previous Pallas | Triton |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | forward | 423.9 us | 226.4 us |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | backward | 1024.3 us | 380.7 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | forward | 103.2 us | 59.3 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | backward | 262.9 us | 105.3 us |

Median kernel time per call on one GB200, 9 documents per sequence. The forward runs at the HBM floor of a read-one-write-one stream on the same tensor, and the backward at 1.14 times its floor. A port of the same algorithm to Pallas reached 230.0 and 403.7 us at C=6144, and needed code-generation workarounds (an inline-asm FMA, program ids clamped to the grid) that steer XLA's Triton pipeline.

The kernel takes kernel size 4, a channel count that is a multiple of 64, and bfloat16 or float32. The wrapper right-pads each local sequence to a multiple of 128 rows with the out-of-range segment id and drops the padded outputs, so any sequence length runs on the kernel. Other calls fall back to `short_conv_reference` with a warning. Every caller gets the kernel, so `GrugModelConfig.sconv_implementation` is removed; checkpoints are unchanged.

The forward and dx are bit-identical to `short_conv_reference` in bfloat16 and float32; dw changes only in fp32 summation order. On SM90 and newer the bf16 multiplies and adds are packed PTX (`mul.rn.bf16x2`, `add.rn.bf16x2`). Older GPUs take an fp32 op and a bf16 cast, which rounds the same way, and Triton's fp fusion is off so that LLVM cannot contract that fallback into a bf16 FMA that rounds once. The fallback has run on GB200 with the capability check forced, but not on an SM80 GPU.

Each program walks a sequence chunk of one channel block. It carries the previous three rows of x (in the backward also the next three rows of dy) and their segment ids in registers, and loads every row of a step before storing any; the backward writes one fp32 dw partial per chunk. A step whose rows lie in one document skips the segment masks, which cuts a backward step from 467 to 275 SASS instructions.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that was 7-15% slower per call shortened the step by 0.55%.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [grug] Keep hero eval and FLOPs metrics continuous across a relaunch
topics.body:
GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len fixes the held-out eval context independently of the training context, so a run that changes context can keep scoring at 4K and its eval_dropless/* series stays comparable. The first-step eval now also runs after a checkpoint resume, once, so each relaunch checks the eval-to-train handoff immediately instead of at the next periodic eval. The dropless eval reports evaluation start and end progress events, as the other evals do.

Per-example FLOPs rise with context length, so the cumulative throughput/total_gflops would jump at a context switch. A FlopsBaseline (completed steps and cumulative FLOPs at the handoff) adds the parent's history to the new shape's count; current MFU uses the new attention cost.

Stacked on #9888. Part of #9615

topics.title: [experiments] Add a JAX collective bandwidth benchmark for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
Add `experiments/amd/collective_ceiling/jax_collectives.py`, which measures the all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce and all-to-all bus bandwidth JAX reaches under `shard_map` across the GPUs of one node, optionally next to an independent matmul. Sizes and bus bandwidth follow the [nccl-tests conventions](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md) that rccl-tests shares, so results compare directly with rccl-tests on the same node.

On 8x MI350X, all-gather reached 392 GB/s for the 1.34 GB message that the June 67B-A2B model's expert-parallel all-gather sends at batch 64, matching rccl-tests ([results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027494656), jobs 453572, 453633, 453651).

Each case compiles, makes one mandatory warm-up call, then makes blocking warm-up calls for `--extra-warmup-seconds` (0 adds none). The mean warm-up call time sets the iterations per timed window, and timed windows dispatch back to back. With `--overlap`, the matmul is timed alone once per run, and overlap rows are logged as effective bus bandwidth because they divide the size by the time of the collective and the matmul together.

The GPU runs above used an earlier revision. Later changes have not been rerun on GPU: `--ops` accepts only known collectives, timing settings pass as a dataclass, the mandatory warm-up call is explicit, extra warm-up calls block before the deadline check, and the overlap matmul is timed once per run.

This code was split out of #9852. It keeps `main` as its base and relies on `experiments/amd/__init__.py` from #9877, so merge it after #9877.

This measures how fast one GPU runs a plain dense matmul, to give the MFU numbers above a measured ceiling. Two tools ran on the same node for each GPU type: k007-002 for MI350X, k002-003 for MI300X. - Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py) (PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_ENABLED=1`, which benchmarks every rocBLAS and hipBLASLt solution per shape and keeps the fastest) searches about 2,100 shapes. It reports MAMF (maximum achievable matmul FLOPS): the median of the 5 fastest of 200 iterations, run in bursts of 20 after 250 ms idle. It also reports MSMF (maximum sustainable matmul FLOPS): the best rate held for 2 s under continuous load. It times each `torch.mm` with GPU events recorded just before and after the call, so its rates count kernel time only.
- `jax_matmul.py` (JAX 0.11.0) times `jax.jit(jnp.matmul)` with XLA autotuning on: 1 s of warmup, then the median of ten 0.2 s windows of back-to-back calls. It runs under `rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` and reports two rates per shape. Kernel time divides the FLOPs by the GPU time of the kernels inside each window, which matches MAMF-finder's timing. Wall clock divides them by host time, which also counts host dispatch and the idle GPU time between calls. Both are sustained rates, so MSMF is the PyTorch number to compare with.

Hardware and theoretical peaks:

| | MI350X | MI300X |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture, compute units | gfx950, 256 CUs | gfx942, 304 CUs |
| Memory per GPU (as torch reports it) | 288 GB HBM3E (294,896 MB) | 192 GB HBM3 (196,592 MB) |
| Dense bf16 and fp16 peak | 2,307 TFLOP/s, as in this issue (brochure: 2,309.6) | 1,307 TFLOP/s (datasheet: 1,307.4) |
| Node, Slurm partition | k007-002, `mi3508x` | k002-003, `mi3008x` |

The peaks are AMD's dense figures without structured sparsity. `lib/fray/src/fray/device_flops.py` stores the brochure values; the percentages below use 2,307 and 1,307 to match the tables above.

Software, identical on both GPUs:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| ROCm user-space libraries | `rocm==10.0.0` wheels (`rocm-sdk-core`, `rocm-sdk-libraries`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx942`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx950`) from `https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/` |
| hipBLASLt, rocBLAS | 100401-8d1ae90e, 5.6.0.8d1ae90e (from TunableOp's results file) |
| PyTorch | 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, with `amd-torch-device-gfx942` and `-gfx950` 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0. `torch.version.hip` is 7.15.26333 and `torch.version.cuda` is None: a ROCm build, no CUDA |
| JAX | jax and jaxlib 0.11.0, `jax_rocm10_plugin` and `jax_rocm10_pjrt` 0.11.0+rocm10.0.0 |
| Kernel tracing | `rocprofv3` from the `rocm-sdk-core` 10.0.0 wheel |
| MAMF-finder | commit [0359db8](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py), benchmark version 4, auto search, default tuning |
| Python, OS | 3.12.12, Linux 5.14.0-611.54.1.el9_7 |
| JAX flags | `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`, `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0`; the Triton-off run adds `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` |

Each run used GPU 0 while the other 7 GPUs on the node were idle.

```bash
sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 60 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/mamf.sbatch --dtype bfloat16"
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 60 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/jax_matmul.sbatch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --m-range 4096 20480 4096 --n-range 4096 20480 4096 --k-range 4096 20480 4096 \
  --shapes-file experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt"
```

Results in TFLOP/s per GPU, with the share of the dense peak. Shapes are MxNxK. The JAX column is kernel time, with the traced wall-clock rate of the same shape in parentheses.

| GPU | dtype | MAMF (PyTorch) | MSMF (PyTorch) | JAX best | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI350X | bf16 | 1,445 (62.6%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 (54.7%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,229 (53.3%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,178) | 453328, 454577 |
| MI350X | fp16 | 1,377 (59.7%) @ 4096x4096x20480 | 1,177 (51.0%) @ 8192x4096x14336 | 1,086 (47.1%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,047) | 453329, 454578 |
| MI300X | bf16 | 698 (53.4%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | 645 (49.3%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | not run | 453334 |

The JAX column covers a 125-shape grid (M, N and K each 4096, 8192, ..., 20480), the June model's projection shapes, and, for bf16, the 28 shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted (job 454579). By kernel time, JAX reaches 97% of MSMF in bf16 and 92% in fp16. Without the tracer, the best bf16 wall-clock rate was 1,192 at 4096x4096x16384 and 1,180 at 4096x4096x12288 (job 453420).

Measured against these ceilings instead of the datasheet, the MI350X baseline above (3.88% MFU, 90 TFLOP/s per GPU) runs at 7.3% of the JAX bf16 kernel-time ceiling. The confirmed MI300X batch-16 row (8.66%, 113 TFLOP/s) runs at 17.5% of PyTorch's MSMF; JAX was not measured on MI300X.

The MI300X run reproduces the MI300X bf16 row in [Stas Bekman's table](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/README.md#maximum-achievable-and-sustainable-matmul-flops-comparison-table) (MAMF 676, MSMF 659, PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0): MAMF is 3.3% higher and MSMF 2.1% lower. His table has no MI350X row. His MI355X row reads 62.6% of peak, the same share as our MI350X MAMF.

The next table times the same matmul shapes in both frameworks, in bf16 on MI350X, using the shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted. MSMF is PyTorch's sustained rate after TunableOp has kept the fastest rocBLAS or hipBLASLt solution for that shape; the TunableOp column names the library it picked. JAX kernel time comes from job 454579, where XLA's autotuner picked a hipBLASLt kernel for every shape. JAX wall clock comes from job 453412, which ran without the tracer.

| Shape | MSMF | TunableOp | JAX kernel | JAX / MSMF, kernel | JAX wall | JAX / MSMF, wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 | rocBLAS | 1,052 | 83% | 1,008 | 80% |
| 4096x4096x8192 | 1,246 | hipBLASLt | 1,209 | 97% | 1,150 | 92% |
| 3584x4608x8192 | 1,237 | rocBLAS | 1,199 | 97% | 1,137 | 92% |
| 4096x4096x20480 | 1,224 | hipBLASLt | 1,179 | 96% | 1,153 | 94% |
| 4096x2048x20480 | 1,089 | hipBLASLt | 1,111 | 102% | 1,065 | 98% |
| 2048x4096x4096 | 1,080 | rocBLAS | 959 | 89% | 828 | 77% |

An earlier version of this comment read the 2-23% wall-clock gap as XLA choosing slower kernels. Most of that gap was the timing method. Wall clock counts host dispatch and the GPU's idle time between calls: on MI350X a trivial jitted op takes about 43 µs to dispatch, and the GPU idles about 12-15 µs between executions even when the host keeps ahead (job 454529). Kernel time removes that overhead. On 2048x4096x4096 it moves JAX from 77% to 89% of MSMF, and on 4096x4096x8192 from 92% to 97%. JAX's kernels are within 4% of MSMF on four shapes. Two gaps remain: 17 points on 4608x4096x7168 and 11 points on 2048x4096x4096. TunableOp picked a rocBLAS solution for both. Every GEMM kernel XLA picked in these runs carries hipBLASLt's `UserArgs` naming, and we have not checked whether XLA's autotuner considers rocBLAS solutions or whether they account for those gaps. TunableOp also picked rocBLAS for 3584x4608x8192, where JAX's hipBLASLt kernel reaches 97%.

On MI350X in bf16, the June model's projection GEMMs at 4096 tokens per GPU run at 369 TFLOP/s (k and v weight gradients, 2560x640x4096) to 1,058 (lm head weight gradient) by kernel time through JAX (job 454577). 4096x2560x2560 is the shape of the q, attention output and shared expert gate, up and down projections, and of their input gradients. It runs at 972 by kernel time and 826 by untraced wall clock (job 454529). The lm head forward runs at 1,030 by kernel time and 1,029 by untraced wall clock. The k and v projections, 4096x640x2560, run at 427 by kernel time with XLA's Triton GEMM and at 556 with hipBLASLt (next table). By untraced wall clock they run at 257 with Triton. Full list in [`snowball_shapes.txt`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt). The routed-expert `ragged_dot` and the small router, attention gate and GatedNorm GEMMs are not covered.

In bf16, XLA generates its own Triton GEMM for four of the k and v shapes: every shape with a dimension of 640, and 2560x1280x4096. Every other shape uses a hipBLASLt kernel. With `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` (job 454580), XLA uses hipBLASLt for these shapes too, and its kernels run 17-33% faster in bf16. Kernel time in TFLOP/s:

| Shape | Use | Triton (454577) | hipBLASLt, Triton off (454580) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4096x640x2560 | k and v projections | 427 | 556 | +30% |
| 2560x640x4096 | k and v weight gradients | 369 | 490 | +33% |
| 2560x1280x4096 | k and v weight gradients, fused | 514 | 664 | +29% |
| 4096x2560x640 | k and v input gradients | 471 | 552 | +17% |

Of the other 38 shapes in the Triton-off run, 33 used the same hipBLASLt kernel as with Triton on, and their kernel time moved by at most 1.6%. For the other 5, the autotuner picked a different hipBLASLt kernel in the new run (see the variation note). Under the tracer, wall clock moved the other way on the four Triton shapes: on 4096x640x2560 a call took 48 µs with Triton and 61 µs with hipBLASLt, against kernel times of 31 and 24 µs, so host-side work sets the wall-clock rate at this size. We have not measured these shapes with Triton off without the tracer. In fp16 (job 454578), XLA also picks Triton for 4096x2560x1280; we did not run fp16 with Triton off.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- fp16 is slower than bf16 for dense matmuls on MI350X: MAMF is 5% lower, JAX 12% lower by kernel time.
- The best 10 JAX grid shapes in bf16 fall between 1,179 and 1,229 TFLOP/s by kernel time (job 454577).
- Run-to-run variation on k007-002. With the same kernel, repeated runs agree closely: across the 24 MAMF shapes where jobs 454579 and 454580 ran the same kernel, the median difference is 0.3% and the largest 0.6%. Some shapes move more. 4096x4096x16384 measured 1,188, 1,221 and 1,189 by kernel time (jobs 454529, 454561, 454577), and 1,192 and 1,153 by untraced wall clock (jobs 453420, 454529). Treat differences of about 3% as noise. XLA's autotuner can also pick a different hipBLASLt kernel for the same shape in a new run. It did so for 4 of the 28 MAMF shapes between jobs 454579 and 454580 and moved three of them by 7-12% (for example 20480x4096x12288: 1,039 with a 192x320 tile in job 454579, 1,164 with a 256x256 tile in job 454580).
- Under `rocprofv3`, wall clock reads lower for shapes that take less than about 100 µs per call, because the tracer adds host work to every dispatch: 4096x1280x2560 reads 401 traced (job 454561) and 472-550 in two untraced passes (job 454529). Wall-clock numbers above say which kind they are.
- The node matters. JAX on MAMF-finder's 28 shapes ran a median of 3% faster on k007-002 than on k007-004 by wall clock, and faster on 26 of the 28 shapes (jobs 453412 and 453338). The two slower shapes, 20480x4096x12288 (-8%) and 16384x8192x8192 (-4%), may reflect XLA's autotuner picking a different kernel rather than the node: 1,043 on k007-002 matches the 192x320-tile kernel in the variation note, and these two runs did not record kernel names. k007-001 and k007-003 have not been compared. The bf16 grid's best wall-clock rate was 1,156 on k007-004 (job 453314) against 1,192 on k007-002.
- With `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, JAX ran bf16 matmuls at 15-17 TFLOP/s, 1% of the autotuned rate (job 453316, stopped by its 45-minute limit after 99 shapes). Any hipBLASLt kernel is far faster than that, so level 0 appears to switch to a different GEMM path on ROCm, and it cannot measure hipBLASLt's untuned default choice.
- MAMF-finder's telemetry on MI350X read the wrong GPU. It samples `amdsmi` GPU 0, but HIP device 0 on k007-002 is PCI 0000:77:00, which is `amd-smi` GPU 3; `amd-smi` GPU 0 is an idle GPU at about 308 W. The MI350X MAMF and MSMF runs (jobs 453328 and 453329) predate the fix in stas00/ml-engineering#143, so their power and clock readings, the 38 MHz and 308 W in their logs, and the "not a boost burst" warning from the MAMF boost check all come from that idle GPU. MAMF-finder's TFLOP/s do not depend on telemetry. On MI300X it reads 750 W and 1,315 MHz sustained and 2,096 MHz at boost, matching the 750 W cap in note 9 of Stas Bekman's table.
- Power cap on MI350X (`amd-smi static --limit`, job 453520): the socket power limit is 1,000 W, equal to the maximum limit and to the brochure's maximum TBP. During a sustained bf16 4096x4096x16384 matmul in JAX (job 453523), the GPU held 1,000 W at a 70-73 °C hotspot, below the 100 °C slowdown temperature, and its 8 compute dies ran at 1,332-1,513 MHz, about 1,400 MHz on average. At 1,400 MHz the peak formula (256 CUs x 4,096 bf16 FLOPs per clock) gives about 1,470 TFLOP/s, 64% of the 2.2 GHz figure. Against that power-limited peak, MSMF is about 86%, JAX by kernel time on the same shape (1,189 in job 454577) about 81%, and JAX by untraced wall clock in job 453523 (1,145 TFLOP/s) 78%. MAMF's short bursts may run above the sustained clock before the GPU reaches its power limit, so the 1,400 MHz figure does not bound MAMF.
- With torch imported, the `amdsmi` Python binding from `/opt/rocm-7.2.0` reports no GPUs, because torch has already loaded the ROCm SDK's own `libamd_smi.so.27`. `setup_envs.sh` uses the SDK's binding instead.
- Next: measure a training step with `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` to see whether the faster hipBLASLt kernels for the k and v GEMMs carry over. Separately, check whether XLA can use the rocBLAS solutions TunableOp picked for 4608x4096x7168 and 2048x4096x4096 (`tunableop-*.csv` in the results directory), and whether those solutions close the remaining gaps.

</details>

Edit: first posted with JAX numbers from node k007-004 while MAMF-finder ran on k007-002. All MI350X numbers now come from k007-002. JAX medians now use the true median of the ten windows. The MI350X telemetry note was corrected after jobs 453520 and 453523 showed MAMF-finder sampling a different GPU. Second edit: JAX now reports kernel time from a `rocprofv3` trace next to wall clock, and comparisons with MAMF and MSMF use kernel time (jobs 454577-454580). This corrects the earlier reading that the wall-clock gap came from XLA's kernel choice; XLA's choice still costs 17-33% on the k and v shapes, where it picks its own Triton GEMM. The Snowball shapes now cover separate k and v projections, the k and v weight gradients and the input gradients, and the paragraph names every projection behind a shared shape. Added the Triton-off comparison, the run-to-run variation note, and the TunableOp library choices. Scripts moved to `experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/`, and the grid arguments are now `--m-range`, `--n-range` and `--k-range`.

### Hiding `ring_dedup`'s synchronous all-to-alls behind the shared expert: no gain

Commit: 3838b71 (local, on the `ring_dedup` base 91286fc) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454847, 454872, 454943 (overlap + latency-hiding scheduler); 454865, 454945, 454949 (latency-hiding scheduler only); 454857, 454892 (baseline)

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton \
  XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Variant (`save_moe`) | Step | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1.589 s | 14.23% | 206.5 GiB |
| latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s (best 1.569) | 14.36% | 207.7 GiB |
| shared expert pinned under the transfers + latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s | 14.36% | 208.2 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What was tried.** A `custom_vjp` around `ring_dedup`'s return `all_to_all` runs the shared-expert MLP between the transfer's start and its use. The backward does the same for the dy `all_to_all` and the shared-expert backward. Ordering is enforced with `optimization_barrier`. The shared expert moves into the backend (`moe_mlp(..., shared_expert=...)`). f32 CPU tests on 8 shards match `ring_dedup` plus a separately computed shared expert to 1e-5 in value and in every gradient.
- **The forward return was already hidden.** In the default schedule the forward return `all_to_all` is async and spans the shared-expert forward GEMMs (30 of 45 ms per profiled step run under it). The synchronous forward transfer is the dispatch. The backward dy `all_to_all` is synchronous.
- **Without the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers backfire.** XLA's default GPU schedule doesn't move all-to-all starts earlier, so it placed the shared GEMMs before the start and every large `all_to_all` became synchronous: 1.610 s vs 1.589 s (+1.3%).
- **With the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers work, but the time just moves.** Unhidden ms per profiled step with the scheduler, before → after pinning:

  | Transfer | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | dy | 41 | 26 |
  | dx | 7 | 33 |
  | forward return | 66 | 90 |

  The scheduler was already hiding dx behind the shared backward. It won't split that work across dy and dx, and scheduling-group annotations, which could force the split, crash the compiler on this ROCm build.
- **`recompute_all`:** baseline 1.707 s, scheduler only 1.695 s, scheduler + pinning 1.703 s.
- **The latency-hiding scheduler alone** gives -0.9% (`save_moe`) and -0.7% (`recompute_all`) here, but an earlier run measured +0.7%. That's within run-to-run noise (about 1.5%), so the defaults stay as they are.
- **Next:** profile-guided latency-hiding scheduling (`xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`), so the scheduler fills windows by measured transfer time; or find other independent work for the forward dispatch window.

</details>

### Re-baseline on `main` (#9832, #9830, #9777) and `ragged_all_to_all` on MI350X: ring numbers unchanged; ragged runs only through XLA's decomposer, 55x slower

Commit: d733cb2 (local: the `ring_dedup` base 91286fc merged with `main` at e11ab28) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 455320, 455339, 455394, 455439, 455430 (re-baseline); 455374, 455386, 455429, 455437 (`ragged_all_to_all`); 455319, 455338 (collective probe); 455382 (tests)

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl <ring|ring_dedup|ragged_all_to_all> [--pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1] --remat-mode <save_moe|recompute_all>
# ragged_all_to_all additionally: XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_unsupported_enable_ragged_all_to_all_decomposer=true
```

| Backend | Remat | Batch | Step | MFU | Peak mem | Drops | Before merge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ring | save_moe | 64 | 1.730 s | 13.07% | 206.0 GiB | 1.01% | 1.730 s |
| ring_dedup (transport 1.1) | save_moe | 64 | 1.582 s | 14.29% | 206.5 GiB | 1.15% | 1.580 s |
| ring | recompute_all | 64 | 1.768 / 1.773 s | 12.78% | 158.0 GiB | 0.96% | 1.798 s |
| ring_dedup (transport 1.1) | recompute_all | 64 | 1.691 s | 13.37% | 158.2 GiB | 0.97% | 1.688 s |
| ragged_all_to_all + decomposer | save_moe | 64 | OOM (534.6 GiB temp) | | | | |
| ragged_all_to_all + decomposer | recompute_all | 16 | OOM (158.2 GiB temp) | | | | |
| ragged_all_to_all + decomposer | recompute_all | 8 | 23.302 s | 0.12% | 190.0 GiB | 6.55% | |
| ring | recompute_all | 8 | 0.420 s | 6.73% | 147.6 GiB | 4.50% | |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **`ring` and `ring_dedup` don't move.** `main` changed no code on their path; its library changes are in `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py`, `sonic.py` and a new `topk.py`. `ring` with `recompute_all` came out 1.5% faster in two runs, which is at the edge of run-to-run noise.
- **FLOPs per example are unchanged at 6.52e13** (5,305,917,440 per token, 7 full-attention layers, from the benchmark's own log). #9633 was already in the base, so every earlier MFU stands.
- **`ragged_all_to_all` without extra flags** fails with `UNIMPLEMENTED: Device communicator is not implementing`, as on MI300X. The backend's `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true` is not a flag in JAX 0.11.0's XLA, so passing it aborts the process. Symmetric buffers, the one-shot kernel flag and every `xla_gpu_ragged_all_to_all_mode` value still return `UNIMPLEMENTED`. The ROCm plugin contains a ragged all-to-all device kernel, but no flag in this build routes the op to it.
- **The decomposer works but is far too slow.** `--xla_gpu_unsupported_enable_ragged_all_to_all_decomposer=true` gives correct results; a single 10.7 MB-per-GPU transfer takes 13.6 ms. In the full model it is 55x slower than ring at batch 8 and runs out of memory at batch 16 and 64. Loss matches ring at batch 8 (11.7922 vs 11.7921 at step 19).
- **#9832's Triton kernels don't run on ROCm.** They go through `jax_triton`, which is only in the CUDA `gpu` extra, so the backend falls back to gathers and zero-filled buffers.
- **#9777 works:** no more `gfx950` parse error. The QuACK path is skipped and `ragged_dot` is used.
- **#9830's routing top-k** used `jax_triton` and served only the hero model, while the June model used #9889's ROCm-only Pallas top-k. #9942 now replaces both with one Pallas-Triton kernel that runs on NVIDIA and AMD: within 1% of #9830's kernel at the hero shape on GB200, and 1.4-3.3x faster than #9889's at the June shape.
- **Tests** (`test_grugformer_moe.py`, single process): 80 passed, 16 skipped, 5 failed. The 5 are the `ragged_all_to_all` tests, which now fail with `UNIMPLEMENTED` instead of the `gfx950` parse error. With the decomposer, 16 of the 17 ragged tests pass. The remaining `test_ragged_moe_reads_no_unwritten_transport_rows_on_gpu` failure turned out to be a test artifact that also reproduces on 8x H100, not a backend bug. Don't export `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton` for this file: its CPU-subprocess tests inherit it and fail.
- `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` from `main` worked unchanged.

</details>

topics.title: [levanter] Stop background iterators after completion
topics.body:
Buffered background iterators now remain stopped after the producer finishes or raises. Previously, consuming the single end marker or error left later `next()` calls waiting forever on an empty queue. Levanter uses this iterator to prefetch data loader batches and evaluation requests.

Regression tests reproduce the hang after normal exhaustion and producer failure in bounded and unbounded queues. The affected safe suite passed 1,063 tests with 13 skips.

topics.title: [grug] Add a Pallas-Triton flash attention for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
Add `gpu_pallas_triton_flash`, an opt-in fused causal attention for Grug on AMD GPUs, where Grug had no fused kernel. Existing backends are unchanged.

The kernel reduces each mask to one inclusive key lower bound per query, `max(segment start, q - W + 1)` for window `W`. Key blocks outside `[lower bound, q]` are skipped, and blocks fully inside it skip the mask computation. GQA indexes the shared KV head instead of repeating K/V. Under a mesh, batch and heads may be sharded; sequence and head_dim may not.

On one MI350X at the June per-GPU shape (8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16), one layer's forward plus backward drops from 18.95 ms to 6.89 ms with a 2048-token window and from 18.98 ms to 10.92 ms causal. The benchmark script is in #9883. The full June model at batch 64 on 8x MI350X goes from 2.426 s to 1.853 s per step (9.32% to 12.20% MFU), peak memory falls from 184 to 158 GiB, and the loss matches the reference run. Details are in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027803714.

Value and gradient parity tests against `reference_attention` pass on MI350X. CI runs them only in the Pallas interpreter, so it never compiles the Triton kernels.

Each run of equal segment IDs is one document, so a segment ID that reappears after a different ID starts a new document; `reference_attention` lets the two runs attend to each other. Masks that carry FA4 precomputed bounds are rejected, which excludes the moe_hero_ep, moe_hero_fsdp and fast_track variants. JAX has deprecated the Pallas Triton backend.

topics.title: [grug] Leave ragged MoE transport rows unwritten when nothing reads them
topics.body:
The ragged all-to-all MoE stops zero-filling and overwriting transport rows that no consumer reads, and on GPU builds its dispatch buffer with one scatter. Outputs, drops and gradients are bitwise unchanged. One MoE layer's forward and backward is 4.4-4.8% faster and its compiler temp 1.37 GB smaller, and the hero step shortens by 1.41% (13.732 to 13.541 s against #9831, over 26 scored steps).

The expert chunks write disjoint rows of the dispatch and return buffers, but the custom VJP around `ragged_all_to_all` differentiated each write as an overwrite, so every layer's backward spent a [TK, H] select, add and zero fill on rows the next chunk would ignore. Each written row holds nothing before its one write, and for such a row an overwrite has the derivative of an add, so the transpose passes the output cotangent through unchanged. With every consumer reading only rows a collective wrote, the buffers need no fill: on GPU they come from a Triton kernel that writes nothing, elsewhere they are zero-filled. Each buffer is tied to a loop-carried value, because XLA would otherwise hoist an input-free buffer out of the layer loop and copy it into every layer's output slot. Dropped and padded slots get combine weight 0, and the combine and dispatch-gradient sums skip them. A GPU test fills every buffer with NaN instead of zero and requires identical outputs, drop counts and gradients under 22 routings, among them an expert no token selects, a receiver chunk and a whole receiver with no rows, a sender with only padding, and near-total drops, with two chunks of three experts per GPU as on the hero.

On GPU, a Triton kernel builds the expert-sorted dispatch buffer by reading each token's row once and writing it to the token's accepted slots, where a gather read every row topk times: 0.535 ms (6.6 TB/s) at the hero's per-GPU routed shape (TK = 524288 rows of the 3072-wide latent). Its weighted form serves #9833's backward. The gather-sum's forward loops over 1024-wide hidden tiles, which keeps more programs resident: 0.508 ms against 0.574 ms.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0), each head compiled fresh.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

comments.body:
🤖 `test_ragged_moe_reads_no_unwritten_transport_rows_on_gpu` fails on 8 GPUs, but the backend is fine: no consumer reads an unwritten transport row.

The test traces the zero-filled and NaN-filled runs as two separate copies inside one jit, then requires bitwise-equal gradients. On 8 GPUs (data axis 4) only the bf16 `w13`/`w2` gradients, the ones summed across data ranks, differ: 6-18% of elements, all finite, max abs difference 0.5-2 (up to a few hundred bf16 ulps on elements near zero, where terms cancel). Filling with `-0.0` instead of NaN gives exactly the same mismatch, and on H100 even static-zero vs runtime-zero differs, so the two compiled copies sum in different orders. Outputs, `grad_x`, combine-weight gradients and drop counts always match.

With one executable that takes the fill value at runtime, every output, drop count and gradient is bitwise equal across fills of 0, NaN and 1e4. We checked:
- 8x H100 with the hero's ragged XLA flags (device kernel, symmetric buffers, `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES`, overlap limit 1, command buffers off), JAX 0.11.1 ([run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdev%2Funwritten-9832-h100x8-heroflags))
- 8x H100 with NCCL's ragged all-to-all, and with XLA's decomposer ([run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdev%2Funwritten-9832-h100x8-c))
- 8x MI350X with the decomposer (Slurm jobs 455382 and 455652 on the AMD HPC Fund cluster)

The test as written fails the same way in each.

Side note: with only `RAGGED_REQUIRED_XLA_FLAGS` set, without `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES`, the test hangs on 8x H100 ([run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdev%2Funwritten-9832-h100x8-reqflags)), matching the comment in the hero's `train.py`.

The diagnostic script and the run scripts are in [this gist](https://gist.github.com/asartran/381f60ec77781cedb88d0fb3e9b2319a).

A fix would compile once and pass the fill as data, e.g. through a `pure_callback` in `_transport_buffer`, since `shard_map` rejects a closed-over Explicit-sharded array. On 2 or 4 GPUs the gradient sum can't reorder, which is probably why the test passes there.

topics.title: [iris] Quarantine nodes with persistent isolated S3 failures
topics.body:
Add bounded S3 write/read/delete probes to the Kubernetes node agent. Each probe uses the task storage endpoint and credentials and writes a small scratch object per node incarnation. The controller cordons persistent outliers only after a fresh majority of nodes successfully probes the same target after the failure began. Node UID, boot ID, report freshness, environment revision, and Kubernetes resource versions fence stale evidence and concurrent changes.

Group checks under `kubernetes_provider.node_health` with a shared cordon budget. The production `cw-rno2a`, `cw-us-east-02a`, and `cw-us-east-08a` configs probe the shared `marin-us-east-02a` bucket under one-day scratch expiry. The node agent continues probing while cordoned. A fresh success from the current node and configured target after the cordon uncordons a node quarantined by Iris and releases its budget, including after a reboot or credential rotation. Operator cordons remain. Running tasks are not evicted.

Health and cordon evidence remain in node annotations when Finelog is unavailable. Configuration, scratch-object lifecycle, and recovery are documented in the CoreWeave guide. The node-local storage failure that motivated this check is recorded in the [hero incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/599).

topics.title: [grafana] Prepare GPU history by requested priority
topics.body:
Prepare seven-day H100 and Blackwell (GB200) allocation-history panels grouped by each child job's requested priority. An Interactive request dispatched as Batch stays in the Interactive group. There is no applied-priority lookup or toggle. Iris and Finelog server code, persisted schemas, retention and writes are unchanged.

The projection sums requested GPU sizes over recorded attempt execution intervals at common sampling instants, with cadence chosen from the selected range: one minute through six hours, five minutes through two days, and fifteen minutes through seven days. Exact historical pod binding/cleanup intervals and allocatable capacity remain unavailable. The requested-GPU series therefore recovers only part of allocation; every point is marked incomplete and idle stays blank. Missing regional inputs leave blank spans. Coverage compares Finelog per-root Running task counts with retained attempt intervals, including CPU tasks; differences flag incomplete or inconsistent task history. It also reports setup tasks and unresolved GPU models. Without assignment creation times, the reader cannot establish when setup began, so setup GPU quantities stay blank.

The production metadata reader remains to be implemented and wired; without one the bridge returns HTTP 503. An approved temporary pilot used Grafana's actual CW service identity plus five-minute Iris dashboard-role cookies over the public Kubernetes controller proxy in all three regions. Existing job/resource/full-retry reads succeeded, GetCurrentUser reported dashboard, and SELECT1 was denied by Iris with HTTP 403. All temporary Role/RoleBinding objects were deleted and absence verified; Grafana's original proxy403 returned afterward. No production grants, credentials or deployment remain from the pilot. The minimal tested transport scope is services/proxy on iris/iris-controller-svc:10000; this reader's POST RPCs need the Kubernetes create verb, plus separate read-only Iris authentication.

A straightforward job/task-API reader would require at least 44,398 inventory calls over the captured sampled cohort, before additional pages and full-retry calls. This is a request-count estimate, not measured production latency. Existing controller backups offer a possible bulk alternative without controller changes: recent backups exist in all three regions. One GB200 backup was 25.4 MB compressed and 421.6 MB decompressed; it downloaded in 1.17s, decompressed in 0.22s, and returned 5,712 retained attempts in a 0.032s immutable local SQL query on devbox. Regional coverage, Cloud Run memory/refresh cost, and scoped object-read credentials still need validation before choosing and wiring that reader. Existing backups already contain requested band and current task band; older attempts do not have their own applied-band field.

All 421 Grafana tests and pre-commit checks passed. The requested-only preview uses captured task-state and regional metadata, with 672 common fifteen-minute instants per model. Every point is incomplete; 226 instants show a difference between per-root Running counts and retained intervals. Earlier applied-view replay timings are retained as prior measurements; production requested-reader loading and refresh costs remain unmeasured.

topics.title: Pod creation fails on a node with 65K empty Silo cgroups
topics.body:
On October 2, new pods failed to start on CoreWeave node `g5bc6da`, blocking new jobs. Kubernetes reported `no space left on device` while creating a pod’s cgroup, the kernel group used to track and limit container resources. The node still reported healthy, and its filesystem had 3.55 TB free.

The host cgroup tree had 65,535 descendant groups. Of these, 65,412 were under `/silo`; that entire subtree contained no processes. This strongly suggests exhaustion of the kernel’s roughly 64K memory-cgroup ID space, though we have not traced the failing allocator.

Silo is the nested container runtime running inside our privileged Iris job `muchanem.cap-pipeline-host-53`. Two sampled container IDs from its `containerd-shim` processes matched empty `/silo` cgroups. This points to a cleanup problem in that workload’s runtime, but we have not identified the code path responsible. We have no evidence that CoreWeave’s host containerd created these groups.

Please investigate whether completed containers leave cgroups and shim processes behind, and fix the cleanup path. Verify that repeated container creation and teardown do not keep increasing either count. Coordinate cleanup of the affected node with the pipeline owner; an empty cgroup alone does not establish that it is safe to remove while the runtime is active.

---

topics.title: [grafana] Bound bridge memory during queries and pod scans
topics.body:
Release query inputs when a cached failure is recorded, and allow at most two dashboard computations, with each slot held from source loading through projection. Cached errors preserve their message and HTTP classification without retaining traceback locals or response bodies. Arrow cache accounting includes full referenced buffers.

Stream Kubernetes pod scans one page at a time and query watched deployments directly for the control-plane crashloop alert. Malformed Kubernetes JSON responses produce HTTP upstream failures rather than partial results. Keep Grafana's Cloud Run memory limit at 4 GiB in Pulumi.

The incident exhausted both the previous 2 GiB limit and a 4 GiB replacement. Local reproductions retained 192 MiB through failed queries in a cache capped at 128 MiB; the change releases those tables. A 2,500-pod synthetic scan fell from 108 MiB to 32 MiB peak Python allocations with identical results. These reproductions establish memory defects; they do not identify every contributor to the production OOMs.

[Incident and reproduction details](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/655).

topics.title: [levanter] Preserve staged mixture indices beyond 2^31
topics.body:
Staged mixtures now preserve child indices when a stage begins after 2^31 samples. Cumulative counts previously used 32-bit storage, and multiplying a stage's block count by samples per block also overflowed before accumulation. Reads in the next stage could therefore use negative child indices.

A regression reads across this boundary through `MixtureDataset.get_batch`. The selected suite reported 1,235 passes, 6 skips, and one parallel worker crash in `test_train_lm_fp8`; that test passed on its isolated rerun.

topics.title: [grug] Hide the hero's bare MoE transports behind shared and chunk GEMMs
topics.body:
Under the hero's carry offload, every MoE transport except one ~1 ms routing-weight return now runs beside a GEMM, which shortens the step by 0.73% (12.730 to 12.638 s) and cuts exposed collective time from 1.19 to 0.85 s/step. Before, with one collective in flight, the first forward dispatch and both recomputed dispatches of the backward ran bare (0.63 s/step), and small collectives inside the routed-MoE section held the slot through expert GEMMs. Three changes that only work together fix the schedule:

- The MLP section's FSDP weight all-gathers, the QB router statistics and the drop count complete before the first dispatch. The statistics are saved for the backward, so its recompute does not rerun their all-reduces.
- The routed MoE runs caller work beside its first dispatch (`DispatchOverlap`), and the block hands it the first shared expert's gate/up projections. Barriers order the remaining transports so that each has an expert or chunk GEMM beside it, in the forward and in the backward's recompute.
- Each layer's carry offload copy starts after the layer's weight slices. XLA puts the 4.3 ms carry copy and the slices on the same memcpy streams in program order, and without this ordering the weight prefetch lands a slice behind the copy and stalls the layer (98-152 ms/step on the production wheel). On #9708's head, disabling only this ordering slowed the step by 0.79%.

Configurations without the carry offload keep the plain path. Neither path is safe under XLA's default scheduler, which can start two transports together, so the launcher refuses a ragged carry-offload run whose XLA flags switch the latency-hiding scheduler off. `forward_barrier` is an `optimization_barrier` whose backward passes cotangents straight through, so a weight gradient's all-reduce and FSDP slice still fuse into a reduce-scatter.

In a four-GPU gate, loss and drop counts are bitwise unchanged and gradients change at rounding level, within the difference between two runs of the same code. In the hero the carry ordering also moves fusion boundaries, so its forward changes at rounding level.

topics.title: [grug] Fuse the expert dSwiGLU and skip recomputed pre-activation stores
topics.body:
Two changes to the routed experts' QuACK kernels, each bitwise or within bf16 rounding:

| Change | Kernel | Hero step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SwiGLU backward and the routing-weight row dot in the dh GEMM's epilogue | 3.54 ms against 5.10 ms per expert chunk | 13.059 to 12.943 s (+0.89%) |
| No gate/up pre-activation store in a forward whose residuals are recomputed | 6.14 ms against 6.48 ms per median chunk, 96 chunks per step | 12.652 to 12.611 s (+0.33%) |

The expert MLP backward wrote dh = dy @ W2^T to HBM and read it back with the gate/up pre-activations in an elementwise pass for the SwiGLU backward and the row dot <h, dh>. A QuACK epilogue on the grouped dh GEMM now unpacks the interleaved (gate, up) tile, applies the SwiGLU backward to the fp32 accumulator, writes the packed (d_gate, d_up) and reduces the row dot, so dh is never materialized. Outputs, drops and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; dx, dW13 and dS change at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp), because the SwiGLU backward runs on the unrounded accumulator.

Under the hero's layer remat, the forward's gated GEMM wrote the [C, 2I] pre-activations of every chunk, which the backward recomputes. `_routed_experts` declares `optimize_remat`, so such a forward runs a primal that calls the expert MLP's new `apply`, which returns the output alone, and the gated GEMM gains a launcher that never writes the pre-activations. Each chunk's dispatch still waits on the previous chunk's gate/up output. The forward is bitwise unchanged, and removing the change from all of #9708 slowed the step by 0.47%.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

topics.title: [grug] Run the production hero with a PGLE latency profile
topics.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

topics.title: [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE backend
topics.body:
This is the top of a three-PR stack. The two PRs below it prepare `ep_ring.py` so this backend can share ring's gather helpers and local assignment selection instead of copying them.

Add `ring_dedup`, an opt-in expert-parallel MoE backend selected with `moe_implementation="ring_dedup"`. `ring` all-gathers every token to every expert shard and reduce-scatters a full-size output. With top-4 of 256 experts over 8 shards, a token reaches 3.3 shards on average, so most of those bytes go to shards that do no work on them.

`ring_dedup` sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its top-4 experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`. A small metadata `all_to_all` carries the combine weights and local expert ids, and a trailer row holds the sender's valid count. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule and the Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32, and returns one row per token. Every hidden-width movement is a gather, so neither pass uses a scatter-add.

The sender capacity per destination is `pooled_transport_capacity_factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing, and `moe_mlp` raises if it is unset. It reuses the `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` parameter so one benchmark flag sets the sender capacity for both backends. The June benchmark sets it with `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` from #9852; 1.1 gave no sender drops. At batch 64 each collective moves 537 MB per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring.

On CPU in f32, the 8-shard tests match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in outputs and gradients, including forced sender drops. At full shapes in bf16 the output differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative, because `ring_dedup` sums in f32. The drop rate is 1.00-1.12%, against 0.93-0.99% for ring.

June Snowball 67B-A2B, 8x MI350X, EP8, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile caches:

| Remat | ring | ring_dedup | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.730 s (13.07% MFU) | 1.580 s (14.31% MFU) | 454012 / 454021 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.798 s | 1.688 s | 454022 / 454026 |

One `ring_dedup` run (job 454010) ran out of memory on GPU 7 at step 5 and hung; its retry passed. That was allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer, which also hits ring at batch 96, and #9901 fixes it with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` in the HPC Fund wrapper. We have not measured `ring_dedup` on TPU or NVIDIA.

Stack, in merge order (each PR is based on the one before):
1. #9860 [grug] Add a gather-only ring EP MoE backend for ROCm (base `main`). Adds the gather helpers `_dispatch_rows` and `_combine_rows` that this backend reuses.
2. #9928 [grug] Move ring's local assignment selection into a helper (base `grug/rocm-ring-combine-top-k`, #9860's branch). Adds `_select_local_assignments`, which this backend calls.
3. #9880 this PR (base `grug/ring-select-local-assignments`, #9928's branch).

The timings above were measured with the ROCm routing top-k from #9889 in place. That kernel is not needed here and is being replaced by #9942. The ring column ran ring with the gather combine, which #9860 now selects with `moe_implementation="ring_gather_combine"`.

topics.title: [zephyr] Abort ThreadedBatchWriter output when the producer fails
topics.body:
When the body of a ThreadedBatchWriter `with` block raised, `__exit__` sent
the normal end-of-stream sentinel. The write function then completed, and
`write_parquet_file` committed the partial file through `atomic_rename`.
Stages that treat an existing output file as "shard done" then skipped the
shard on a re-run and kept the partial output. The normalize main/dups writer
and the datakit quality writer use this pattern.

`__exit__` now sets an abort event before it wakes the thread. The next read
of the write function's stream raises `WriterAbortedError`, so `atomic_rename`
removes its temporary file and nothing is committed. A normal close is
unchanged.

The datakit quality stage in #9694 removes partial outputs after the fact
(`_discard_outputs`); with this change, that code is not necessary.

topics.title: [grug] Add a one-GPU Grug attention layer benchmark

topics.title: [eval] Iris retries overwrite completed run records
topics.body:
An Iris retry can reuse an evaluation's serialized `EvaluationIdentity.run_id` and `output_dir`. The replayed Evalchemy process then appends samples and overwrites `record.json` under an already sealed result URI. A tracker link can therefore change its score after it has been sealed.

Reproduce:
1. Submit an evaluation batch through `experiments/evaluation/launch.py` and let an Evalchemy process finish and seal its FineStore archive.
2. Cause Iris to classify the parent task or Evalchemy child task as retryable after that write, such as a post-completion `PodDeleted` or worker preemption.
3. Observe that the replay has a new Iris attempt or child-job ID but writes to the original FineStore path and run-level `record.json`.
4. Compare the first completed attempt, replayed attempt, and current record at that URI.

Expected: an Iris retry must preserve completed results as immutable artifacts. It should either skip a successfully sealed evaluation or allocate attempt-specific run IDs and output paths. A later failed attempt must not downgrade or replace an earlier succeeded record.

Confirmed examples:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261003-210313-Aleph-Alpha-Kolibri-1-mbppplus-b75b/results` first completed at 262/378 (`0.6931216931`). A parent-task retry ran a second MBPP+ child against a new serving endpoint and wrote 274/378 (`0.7248677249`) to the same path. The current `record.json` and FineStore view report the second score.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261002-002728-laion-snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203-gpqa-diamond-5b7b/results` changed from `0.636` to `0.5993265993` after a parent `WORKER_FAILED` retry replayed GPQA-Diamond against a new serving child.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-nupa-9a91/results` held a sealed 5,000-item attempt with 2,414 correct answers (`0.4828`). Iris classified the completed Evalchemy child attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted`, retried the same task and path, and the final canonical record became `0.4788`.
- The Kolibri retry also changed MATH500 from `0.984` to `0.992` and HumanEval+ from `0.774` to `0.7682926829` under unchanged result URIs. When the retried parent was later killed, several earlier succeeded Kolibri `record.json` files were rewritten as `infra_failed`.

`_run_id()` is evaluated while constructing the batch in `experiments/evaluation/launch.py`; Iris retries replay the serialized batch. `write_record()` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py` then writes unconditionally to `{prefix}/{run_id}/record.json`.

comments.body:
🤖 Trinity Mini NUPA provides a child-task-level reproduction and rules out partial aggregation.

The Iris child `/benfeuer/eval-20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-a679/eval-nupa-cb8a6a13/0` has three attempts:

- Attempt 0 completed on 2026-10-02 at 06:24:54 UTC, then Iris recorded `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted` and scheduled a retry.
- Attempt 1 wrote and sealed a complete 5,000-item `NUPA5K-Loose` archive. The archive had 4,510 scored responses, 490 classified infrastructure failures, and 2,414 correct answers, so the recovered score was 2,414 / 5,000 = `0.4828`. The tracker sealed that complete attempt on 2026-10-03.
- Iris again recorded the attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` and started attempt 2 at 2026-10-03 10:41:20 UTC. Attempt 2 completed successfully on 2026-10-04 at 15:46:05 UTC and wrote `0.4788` to the same result URI.

Both reported scores cover the full 5,000-item panel. The difference is between complete replays of one stochastic evaluation under one run ID, not between a partial and final aggregate.

🤖
# Research

`build_evaluation_batch()` serializes one `run_id` and results path per evaluation. An Iris replay enters the same runner with that identity; the evaluator can reopen the sealed archive, and `write_record()` overwrites the canonical record. The September 27 and October 6 incidents document successful records replaced by retry or cancellation failures.

**Relevant code**
- [`launch.py#L213-L220`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L213-L220) — serializes the run ID and results path
- [`runner.py#L243-L269`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L243-L269) — reuses the path and writes a record
- [`records.py#L319-L325`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L319-L325) — replaces `record.json`
- [`store.py#L175-L181`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py#L175-L181) — reopening clears the seal

# Attempt isolation and first-success publication

[PR #9813](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9813) already changes evaluation scheduling and uses `StepSpec` status to skip successful steps on restart. Its own description identifies the remaining crash window between writing a record and marking the step successful. This plan belongs in that PR or its successor; a separate runner PR would overlap it.

## Design

Keep the launch `run_id` as the stable tracker identity. Allocate a fresh attempt ID when an evaluation actually starts, and write Evalchemy or Harbor output, its FineStore archive, and an attempt record under `{records_prefix}/{run_id}/attempts/{attempt_id}/`. Pass that attempt's results path to the executor, so a retry cannot reopen an earlier sealed archive. Preserve the attempt ID and Iris job IDs in the attempt record for audit.

Publish `{records_prefix}/{run_id}/record.json` only after an attempt's output is sealed and its metrics are validated. Use a storage-conditional update (GCS generation or S3 ETag/create precondition) so the first successful record wins even if a lock expires or two writers race. Failure records may replace an earlier failure while no success exists; after success, later attempts cannot replace the canonical record or its referenced results. A replay that finds a canonical success should return that record path before starting serving or evaluation, including when a previous worker died after publication but before `StepSpec` wrote `SUCCESS`.

Update the launcher, runner, record writer, reporting path, and EvalDash reader together. Existing run pages keep the stable `run_id`; the canonical record points at an immutable attempt's results. Keep old flat-layout records readable for historical runs. A deliberate new evaluation gets a new launch `run_id` instead of changing an existing score.

## Costs and risks

The additional attempt directory and conditional publication path change the persistent layout and require both CoreWeave S3 and GCS semantics to be exercised. Step status and record publication can disagree after a crash; recovery must treat a canonical success as complete. Existing readers that assume results live directly under `{run_id}/results` need updating.

## Testing and completion

Add a regression that publishes a successful, sealed attempt, interrupts before step success, then replays the batch: no new evaluator runs and the canonical record and seal remain byte-for-byte unchanged. Cover failure-then-success, success-then-failure, and two competing publishers; verify that attempt records remain separate and EvalDash keeps the first successful score. Run the repository's local evaluation tests and pre-commit checks, then exercise conditional publication on the configured S3 and GCS backends before landing.

## Open question

Should the canonical path show the latest failed attempt until a success arrives, or should failed attempts appear only in the attempt history? The first option preserves current failed-run visibility; either choice must prevent a failure from replacing success.

topics.title: [grug] Add a gather-only ring EP MoE backend for ROCm
topics.body:
Add a `ring_gather_combine` MoE implementation: the ring expert-parallel backend with its dispatch and combine done as gathers in both directions. `ring` keeps the scatter-add combine, and `implementation=None` still resolves to `ring` on every platform. ROCm runs opt in with `moe_implementation="ring_gather_combine"`.

On AMD GPUs the combine `zeros_like(x_global).at[token_local].add(...)` and the transpose of the dispatch `jnp.take` compile to scatter-adds that run at about 0.8-1.2 TB/s. `ring_gather_combine` builds an inverse map from each (token, k) assignment to the dispatch slot that holds it. The dispatch take and the combine get custom VJPs, so both directions are gathers: each token sums its at most K slot rows in f32 (K = 4 in the June model). The combine output is bit-identical to an f32 scatter-add rounded to bf16. `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local` takes the dispatch and combine pair as an argument, and `moe_mlp` binds it when it picks the backend, so the ring code has no platform check. The combine's profile scope is renamed from `scatter` to `combine`, the name the other EP backends use.

topics.title: [grug] Run the shared experts' SwiGLU in QuACK GEMM epilogues
topics.body:
The hero's shared experts run their gate/up and down projections as QuACK GEMMs with SwiGLU and its backward in the epilogues: forward and backward of one shared expert take 13.93 ms instead of 14.51 ms at the hero's per-GPU shape (65536 tokens, width 6144, intermediate width 3072). Removing the change from all of #9708 slows the step by 0.35% and 0.22% in two pairs of runs.

With every PR of this stack and #9829, one 64-GPU hero rack ran 12.590 s/step (31.18% MFU), against 13.899 s (28.24% MFU) for main at #9708's base, with loss within 4.9e-4 of a run of #9708.

Each shared expert runs as two per-shard ops: a gate/up GEMM against interleaved weights with SwiGLU in its epilogue, returning the pre-activations and h, and a down op whose backward runs the SwiGLU backward in the dh GEMM's epilogue. dx and the gate/up weight gradient are single GEMMs on the interleaved layout. The split keeps the gate/up projection movable, so #9835 can run the first shared expert's gate/up beside the first dispatch. The weights stay separate FSDP leaves, gathered inside the shard map, so their gradients still reduce-scatter. Without QuACK, for another activation, or for operands other than bfloat16, the same ops run as XLA einsums.

Since only the down op reads h, the gate/up op stops h's gradient; otherwise the dispatch overlap would hand back dense zeros for h and the backward would run a SwiGLU backward over [T, 2I] per layer that adds nothing. SwiGLU now runs on the fp32 accumulator. Against an fp32 reference in a 4-GPU model gate, the loss error moves from 5.1e-5 to 4.5e-5 and the shared-expert gradient error from 1.22e-2 to 1.15e-2.

Directly on #9835 the change measured -0.11% (12.638 to 12.652 s): there the shared GEMMs cover the transports, and the shorter GEMMs left 0.24 s/step more transport exposed. Measured without #9835 it gained 0.72%, with peak HBM 123.4 to 121.9 GiB.

The QuACK availability check moves to `levanter.grug._moe.availability` and asks the default device for its platform. The shared experts' kernel selection calls it outside the ragged backend, where a test that stubs `jax.default_backend` on CPU devices would make the old check's `jax.devices("gpu")` raise.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

topics.title: [datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps
topics.body:
Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf, and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the `QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw scores: one
Zephyr task per normalized shard on GPU workers, tokenizing the text through the
tokenize stage's own core and reading the Harrier embedding by position. The Nemotron
tokenize leaves the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's
scores are registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than
rescored; a rerun of the score stage lands at the step's own identity. The
content-type leaves written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen step so the
score step can depend on it.

Every input leaf of a source holds the normalized shard's documents in its row
order. A census over all 162,535 shards of the 292 sources found every
fusion-score, content-type and Harrier shard in exactly the normalized order, with
the same ids and row counts. Both steps therefore read their side inputs by
position and check each batch's ids against the normalized shard, so a leaf from a
different normalize run fails its shard. `QualityScores.samples_output_dir` is
removed; the stage report reads its spot-check text from the normalized shard of
the same basename.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`, relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE, frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta. `QualityPin` carries
separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration file, checked by the
worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the bucketed dataset without
moving or rescoring the raw scores. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources. The fusion checkpoint's
document-embedding weights form one optional `DocFusion` submodule whose field
order matches the serialized leaves, so the deployed checkpoint loads to identical
weights and scores, and the calibration file parses into a `Calibration`
dataclass.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12 sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage run from text against the
same embeddings matched the pinned scores to a maximum difference of 1.6e-3 (mean
2.3e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of a 4,096-document batch against the
earlier 32,768.

topics.title: [eval] Check in the September evaluation campaign
topics.body:
Check in the model, evaluator, and launcher configurations for the September 2026 evaluation campaign, together with the runtime fixes needed for serving, retry, resume, and coverage. The launcher validates external pins, writes immutable effective-config snapshots, and accepts an optional submitter-controlled version label. That label does not attest policy conformance.

Harbor results are bound to the full model and hosted judge configurations, dataset, policy, runtime, and task limit. Resume checks this identity before submission and reuse. A changed checkpoint under the same served name is rejected, as are existing roots without model-bound provenance. Recovery retries known infrastructure failures and unscored trials while retaining scored outcomes and unknown errors.

The frozen Harbor runtime pins 94b118022fe3e677784a638daf33d57a836fa5fe and includes the Tau3 adapter. The Evalchemy lock and generated pin match Marin's external dependency configuration.

SWE-bench uses the native Mini-SWE adapter from merged [Harbor #232](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/232) and [#233](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/233). Its 32,768-token context includes the prompt and reply together. Mini-SWE counts the rendered prompt through the serving tokenizer, including tools and the generation prefix, and caps the reply within the remaining budget and server window. Harbor loads Mini-SWE's base configuration before applying overrides and selects its batch agent, which saves the trajectory on context exhaustion without prompting. Harbor can then verify the existing patch.

Sotopia uses the packaged agent from merged [Harbor #231](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/231). Judge failures become verifier infrastructure errors. The Marin agent wrappers and their harness dependencies are removed. Sotopia's native generation still does not enforce its declared context budget, so those results cannot establish conformance to the 32K context policy.

Part of #9566.

topics.title: [grug] Correct hero remat and collective scheduling; build PGLE profiles
topics.body:
Carry-offloaded hero runs stop recomputing ~10 GiB of backward values per step that already fit in HBM, which shortens the step by 1.04% (13.874 to 13.732 s against #9830 on one 64-GPU hero rack, restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps). Ragged runs without the carry offload run their collectives one at a time, and `pgle_profile` builds an XLA PGLE profile from one trace of the train step. No model code changes.

With the layer carry offloaded to pinned host memory, XLA's `HloRematerialization` charged the 36 GiB carry stack against the device memory limit and recomputed values that fit (143 remat clones, 0.63 s/step of compute). The launcher now defaults `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading=true` whenever the carry is offloaded, so remat counts host buffers as host memory. Only the remat pass reads the flag, after scheduling and copy insertion, so it cannot reorder the carry reload against its consumer. The flag also lets remat offload values to host itself when its estimate of the step exceeds its budget, and that path aborts compilation in XLA's `OffloadInstruction` (hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118) when it picks the operand of a collective still in flight. At memory fraction 0.75 and slop factor 85 the budget is 87.7 GiB and remat estimates the step at 96.8 GiB, so the hero crashed at compile. The carry offload therefore also defaults to 0.78 and 105, a 114 GiB budget, and remat then leaves the step alone ("Rematerialized 0 instructions").

A ragged run without the carry offload keeps the latency-hiding scheduler off, and the collective overlap limit binds only that scheduler, so XLA's default scheduler can start two ragged transports at once. Compiled for a mocked EP64 topology, the program does so in the forward and in the backward, and on GB200 several collectives in flight have hung the ragged transport or given run-to-run different gradients. The launcher now forces `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES` for that configuration.

XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so with one collective in flight it treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under one GEMM. A profile built by `pgle_profile` from the program's own trace shortened the hero step with all of #9708 from 12.611 to 12.515 s (+0.77%). A profile applies only to the program it was traced from, so nothing uses one by default; the README describes the trace, build and rerun loop, and #9879 tracks using one in production.
