topics.title: [grug] Add a Pallas-Triton routing top-k for ROCm
topics.body:
On ROCm, `QBRoutedMoE` routing replaces `jax.lax.top_k` with a Pallas-Triton kernel that runs once per token shard. TPU, NVIDIA and expert counts that are not a power of two keep `jax.lax.top_k`.

On AMD GPUs, `jax.lax.top_k` over the `[tokens, experts]` router matrix lowers to rocprim radix sorts. The kernel reads each router row once and runs K rounds of max plus lowest index of the max over total-order integer keys. Its indices match `lax.top_k`, ties and NaNs included. Values are gathered outside the kernel, so gradients match `lax.top_k`.

On one MI350X at the June per-GPU shape, top-5 of 256 over 32,768 tokens takes 0.048 ms against 0.435 ms for `lax.top_k` (`bench_grug_ring_combine_top_k.py`, job 453908). The full June model with this kernel and the gather combine from #9860 went from 1.823 to 1.735 s per step under `save_moe` remat (jobs 453972 / 453979) and from 1.848 to 1.788 s under `recompute_all` (jobs 453841 / 453957); #9860 has the table.

On 8x MI350X (job 454059), `test_routing_top_k.py` passes 13 of 13. Under `JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu` the interpreter tests pass and the ROCm tests skip. In the same job, `test_grugformer_moe.py` has 5 failures, all ragged all-to-all tests: `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` cannot parse `gfx950` as a compute capability. The same 5 tests fail on `main` (job 454060). On this branch, `test_routing_top_k.py` and the ring and routing tests in `test_grugformer_moe.py` pass on 8x MI350X (22 tests, job 454671), and after the fallback fix `test_routing_top_k.py` passes 14 of 14 (job 454870).

The dispatch selection `top_k` and the QB threshold `top_k` still use rocprim sorts, about 12 ms and 8 ms per step.

topics.title: [grug] Let the hero launch use the carry-offload memory budget
topics.body:
`trigger_hero.sh` passed `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.75` and `--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor=85` to the hero coordinator. Since #9831, `_apply_hero_ep_runtime_defaults` gives the hero's carry-offload configuration a 0.78 memory fraction and slop factor 105 together with `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading`. topics.title: [grug] Exit instead of hanging when a June train step stalls
topics.body:
GrugTrainerConfig.step_timeout arms Python's faulthandler timer around each train step
except the first one in the process, which compiles, and watch steps,
which can compile a variant. If a step runs past the timeout, the
process dumps every thread's traceback and exits with status 1. The
default is None, which leaves training unchanged. The synthetic
benchmark sets it with --step-timeout: 300 s by default, 0 disables it.

When one GPU fails inside a step, for example because the BFC allocator
cannot place the step's temp buffer, the other GPUs wait in XLA's
per-step collective rendezvous. On ROCm with JAX 0.11 that rendezvous
never times out. The Python thread blocks on the step's outputs, and the
job sits until its Slurm time limit. In a forced out-of-memory run with
the flag, the job exited 120 s after the out-of-memory error.

Stacked on #9852, which adds the neighboring --watch-interval flag.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [grug] Share one Pallas-Triton routing top-k across NVIDIA and AMD
topics.body:
The routing top-k kernel in `levanter.grug._moe.topk` is now written in Pallas Triton, so it runs on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and no longer needs `jax_triton`. It keeps the #9830 algorithm: one warp per row, the row held as one power-of-two tile or three equal ones (a 384-wide row needs no padding), and k rounds of "largest total-order key, then lowest column". Grug MoE routing (`QBRoutedMoE`) now calls it per token shard in place of `jax.lax.top_k`. The hero model imports the same function and is unchanged. Rows of 1,024 or more, non-float32 inputs and non-GPU backends still use `jax.lax.top_k`.

Per-call time in ms, with 16 calls in one executable, median of 5 runs:

| shape, k | GPU | `lax.top_k` | Pallas (this PR) | `jax_triton` (#9830) | Pallas 64-row (#9889) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | GB200 | 0.837 | 0.0760 | 0.0754 | n/a |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | H100 | 1.107 | 0.0947 | 0.0954 | n/a |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI300X | 0.834 | 0.0656 | n/a | n/a |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI350X | 0.990 | 0.0561 | n/a | n/a |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | GB200 | 0.229 | 0.0201 | 0.0207 | 0.0659 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | H100 | 0.308 | 0.0223 | 0.0238 | 0.0712 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI300X | 0.356 | 0.0246 | n/a | 0.0334 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI350X | 0.414 | 0.0167 | n/a | 0.0288 |

On GB200, H100, MI300X and MI350X the indices equal XLA:CPU's `lax.top_k` for widths 37 to 1,000 and k up to 37, on random, tied, constant, ±0, ±inf and NaN rows. ROCm's own `lax.top_k` departs from the IEEE total order: it ties -0 with +0 and orders NaN payloads differently. On those rows the kernel matches XLA:CPU and CUDA instead, so the GPU tests now compare against `lax.top_k` on the CPU backend.

topics.title: [grug] Keep AdamH updates finite on zero-norm matrices
topics.body:
scale_by_adamh projects onto the parameter's Frobenius sphere by dividing by
the updated matrix norm. A zero matrix stays zero through a zero learning-rate
or zero-gradient step, so the division is 0/0 and the update is NaN. Floor
that norm at 1e-10, the same floor the direction step already uses.

Fixes #9054

topics.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
topics.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. topics.body:
🤖 **Marin Belay Intake: post research suggestions for [Marin Belay v1 (#9451)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451) here.**

Marin Belay is an agent-run experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, fixed 8-minute 8×H100 budget). The agent reads and acts only on the main thread (#9451), which is limited to users with write access. Suggestions from anyone else come in through this issue:

1. **Post your suggestion as a comment here.** One idea per comment, with a paper link or a short rationale if you have one.
2. **A maintainer reviews it.** When a member of the `marin-devs` team reacts with 👍, an automated workflow (every ~5 minutes) copies the comment verbatim into #9451, attributed to you and linked back here.
3. **The workflow then adds 🚀 to your comment**, meaning it has been transferred. It transfers each comment once; editing a comment after the 🚀 does not re-send it.

Suggestions that are off-topic, duplicate existing work, or ask the agent to do anything other than ML research on the ladder won't be approved. The main thread's Status section lists what has been tried and the current best recipe.

Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

topics.title: [grug] Add hero launch controls for a context-length switch
topics.body:
The scaling-ladder launcher takes --seq-len and holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, and gate/router weight decay therefore match the 4K run. A changed context requires an explicit --qk-mult, applied to all attention layers; --capacity-factor overrides the expert receiver capacity. A resume at a new context also requires --context-switch-step and --flops-baseline-step/--flops-baseline-total. The new prior_contexts argument of harrier_mix_2026_08_18_data_config turns the switch step into LmDataConfig.prior_phases, with the Harrier stage schedule at the 4K batch size and the 4K shuffle blocks, so the Harrier sources continue from their 4K reads. Hero eval stays at 4K packing. A context switch is rejected for runs below the 1e23-FLOP simulated-epoching cutoff, because the data offsets assume each source reads its whole cache.

trigger_hero.sh records the context, batch, QK multiplier, capacity, eval context, FLOPs baseline, and context switch step in the W&B lineage and the #8506 launch record.

The live run is unchanged: trigger_hero.sh still launches at 4K. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

topics.title: [levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch
topics.body:
Harrier's shuffle blocks change from a fixed 256 sequences to a fixed 2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K the two are identical, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer context, the token-sized blocks keep the outer block permutation the same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle window changes. With the old 256-sequence blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T.

The new LmDataConfig.prior_phases describes the earlier context lengths of a resumed run. With prior_phases set, each source skips the unread rest of the shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a change in the active sources is rejected. The offsets come from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at 16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

topics.title: [grug] Select the hero router's top-k experts with a Triton kernel
topics.body:
The hero router's top-(K+1) expert selection runs in a Triton kernel instead of a full XLA sort of every row: 0.096 ms per call instead of 0.856 ms at [65536, 384], k = 9 on one GB200, once in the forward and again in the recompute. The indices and their order match `jax.lax.top_k` bitwise for every input, including ties, signed zeros, infinities and NaNs.

XLA:GPU uses its own top-k kernel only for rows of at least 1,024 elements, so 384-expert rows fall back to a sort. The new kernel takes float32 rows narrower than 1,024 on a GPU device; everything else keeps `jax.lax.top_k`. Its gate asks the default device whether it is a GPU, because a hero test stubs `jax.default_backend` to trace a GPU-only path on CPU devices. The Triton gather-sum's gate makes the same check.

One warp holds one row in registers, as one power-of-two tile or, when that pads less, three equal ones (a 384-wide row is three 128-wide tiles), and takes k successive maxima over XLA's float32 total-order key, breaking ties by the lower column. A row in one warp keeps both reductions inside the warp; Triton reduces across warps through shared memory. A taken or absent entry gets the smallest key and the column n, which the lowest-column reduction never returns, so a negative NaN with payload 0xFFFFFFFF, whose key is also the smallest, is not mistaken for one. The kernel reads an int32 view of the input, so autodiff never asks it for a JVP rule. For k above 16 the steps run in a loop, which compiles in 0.2 s where unrolled steps take 36 s at k = 384.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that took 0.125 ms per call shortened the step by 0.53%.

# Independent forecast of the Marin 535B-A23B hero run's final loss: pre-registration v2

- **Frozen:** 2026-10-09 (v2). This supersedes v1 (tag `prereg-2026-10-09`, frozen earlier the same day), which stays public and unchanged.
- **Data:** the same public-data snapshot as v1, taken at 04:40 UTC, with data through step 227,999 of 390,251 (58.4% of training). At 06:06 UTC the run was at step 229,145 and had logged no newer eval. v2 therefore sees exactly the data v1 saw, and only the method changed.
- **Why a v2:** after publishing v1 we re-audited it line by line (code, numbers and text) and re-ran the backtests. Several modeling choices were not supported by the backtests or the data, and the v1 document had several errors. Section 6 lists every change and Section 7 the errata.
- **Author:** Qirun Li (GitHub @bethehand). The analysis was done with the help of Claude (Anthropic) as a coding and analysis assistant.
- **Hero run:** marin-community/marin [#8435](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8435).
- **Freeze record:** SHA-256 hashes of every frozen file are in `results/v2/freeze_manifest_v2.json`.

## 1. Forecast

| Target (final eval, 4K eval packing) | Median | 80% interval | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`, 16 subsets (primary)** | **2.035** | **[2.023, 2.047]** | **[2.016, 2.054]** |
| Same macro over 15 subsets, excluding PTB (companion) | 2.047 | [2.036, 2.059] | [2.030, 2.065] |

Where the team's point forecasts fall in our predictive distribution for the primary target:

| Team forecast | Value | Percentile in our distribution |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-registered, Aug 19 (#8435) | 2.039 | 68th |
| Swap-adjusted, Sep 14 (W&B) | 2.027 | 20th |
| Refit with fitted floors, new mix, Oct 3 (W&B) | 2.100 | above all 60,000 draws; P(final ≥ 2.07) = 0.0002 |

**In short:** the run is on track to finish at or slightly below the Aug 19 pre-registration. Our median is 0.004 below it. A final loss near 2.10 is very unlikely if the run completes as planned. v1 had a median of 2.045; Section 4 shows where the 0.010 difference comes from.

Trajectory forecasts for every 1% from 59% to 100% are in `results/v2/trajectory_official_macro16_v2.csv` and `trajectory_macro15_v2.csv`. Selected points for the primary target:

| Progress (step) | 70% (273,175) | 80% (312,200) | 90% (351,225) | 100% (390,250) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Median | 2.112 | 2.085 | 2.060 | 2.035 |
| 80% interval | [2.105, 2.118] | [2.077, 2.093] | [2.050, 2.070] | [2.023, 2.047] |

## 2. Conditions and scoring rules (fixed in advance)

**Targets**
- **Primary:** `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` at 4K eval packing, read at the final eval of the hero run's W&B lineage (`hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` → … → the current run).
- **Rollbacks:** if part of the run is rolled back and re-run, the value produced by the re-run counts at each step. If W&B keeps the pre-rollback rows instead (as after the Sep 3 rollback within one run, #8506), we use the value the team reports for the re-run; if there is none, we score the next eval after the replayed range.
- **Companion:** the mean of the 15 `eval_dropless/paloma/<subset>-llama3/loss` values, excluding `ptb-llama3`.
- **Steps and fractions:** an eval logged at step s sits at fraction p = (s + 1)/390,251. The final step of the planned schedule is 390,250. Trajectory quantiles are interpolated linearly in p between the rows of the trajectory files. Those rows are every 1%, plus two rows just before and at step 362,280 (see condition 5).

**Conditions**
1. **The run trains at 4K context to the end of the planned 390,251-step schedule:** we score the final eval against the end-of-run distribution.
2. **The training context is extended before the end** (the plan in #9615):
   - Primary score: the last eval before the switch, against our trajectory at that fraction. The team's Aug 19 trajectory (per-5% points, interpolated linearly) is scored at the same eval.
   - The end-of-run value is reported but not scored. If the eval stays pinned at 4K (#9890), we also report the gap between the end-of-run value and our 4K counterfactual.
3. **The token horizon or the learning-rate schedule changes** (shortened, as the policy in #8435 allows, or lengthened):
   - Primary score: the last eval before the schedule changes, against our trajectory.
   - Secondary comparison, for a shortened run that completes its decay: the table in Section 4. For example, ending at 80% gives a median of 2.047.
4. **PTB is dropped from the macro, or the macro definition changes:** the companion target becomes primary.
5. **The eval to be scored falls in the acute window of a PTB exposure:**
   - **The known reads.** #9874 maps the steps at which the hero reads the Paloma PTB text under the current data order: steps 209,390–209,669 (passed) and 362,280–362,578 (ahead, during the cooldown). An exposure's window runs from its start through 12,000 steps after its end. For the second read that is steps 362,280–374,578.
   - **Further copies.** #9874 also notes another PTB copy (n-gram tables, around step 206,300) that its mapping does not cover. It probably caused the dip at eval 206,999, which came before the mapped read. If the team maps that copy, or identifies any other exposure, its window applies too.
   - **Data order changes.** A datamix update under #8435's shortening policy, or a skip to the next shuffle window at a sequence-length change (#9615), can move or remove these reads. Then the windows follow the team's re-mapped steps.
   - Inside a window we score the companion target at that eval and report both.
   - The window is deliberately longer than the effect seen around the first read: three evals (206,999–212,999) sat 0.14–0.34 below the trend, and #9874 reports that the effect had faded by step 216,000.
6. **Any other change to the eval set or eval packing:** only evals before the change are scored.

**Scoring**
- Coverage: does the realized value fall inside the 80% and 95% intervals?
- At the end of the run: the CRPS of our predictive distribution, computed from the frozen Monte Carlo samples in `results/v2/end_samples_v2.npz`, against the absolute error of each team point forecast. For a point forecast CRPS equals the absolute error, so the comparison is like for like.
- At a trajectory point (conditions 2 and 3): the quantile score, 2 × the mean pinball loss over our five frozen quantiles (2.5/10/50/90/97.5%). For a point forecast it also equals the absolute error.
- v2 is the scored forecast. We will report v1's score alongside it.
- The outcome will be published whether the forecast turns out good or bad.

**Mid-course update**
At 70% (step ~273,175) we will re-run the frozen v2 code on new data and post an addendum. It will give:
- the PIT of each new eval under the trajectory distribution;
- how many new evals fall in the 80% band;
- the re-estimated residual slope b.

The scored forecast remains the frozen one.

## 3. Method

**Anchoring.** We use the scaling ladder only for *how much more the loss will fall from now to the end*. The level comes from the hero's own evals:

```
final = f(1) + a + κ·b·(1 − p_now) + ε − β + η
```

- **f(p):** the hero trajectory predicted from the ladder. It uses the same per-5% log-space fits as the team's pre-registration (`L = E + A·C^(−α)` with E fixed), smoothed with a cubic in p over 30%–100%.
- **a, b:** offset and slope of the hero's residuals against f. They are fitted on the 38 evals with p ≥ 0.299 (steps 116,999–227,999). The data swap was at step 108,000; the two post-swap evals before the cutoff (steps 110,999 and 113,999) are left out.
- **κ ~ U[0, 0.2]:** how much of the observed residual drift persists (v1: U[0, 1]). It is set by backtest: 0.2 is the largest κ whose RMS error over the 15-subset pseudo-heroes is within 10% of the minimum.

  | κ | 0 | 0.1 | 0.15 | 0.2 | 0.3 | 0.5 | 1 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | RMS error | 0.0066 | 0.0050 | 0.0049 | 0.0053 | 0.0072 | 0.0127 | 0.0284 |

- **ε:** method error, Student-t with 8 degrees of freedom and scale 0.0054 (SD 0.0062). The scale is the RMS backtest error (Section 4), taken around zero rather than around the distance trend below, which errs on the wide side.
- **β:** distance-bias allowance, β ~ U[0, b(d)]. Here b(d) is the backtest error trend evaluated at each ladder's extrapolation distance: 0.0072 at 337× (GB200) and 0.0106 at 1,890× (H100). See "Extrapolation distance" below.
- **η:** eval noise at the final eval, SD 0.0031 for the 15-subset target.
- **On the trajectory:** ε and β describe errors in the remaining drop, so they enter in proportion to (p − p_now)/(1 − p_now). The shortened-horizon table applies them in full, because there the run's own end is the target.

**Ladders and the d2048 extension.**
- GB200 d768–d2048 has weight 0.75 and the same batch-scaling recipe as the hero.
- H100 d512–d1536 on the new mix has weight 0.25 and a similar data schedule: its mix switches at 25% of training, against the hero's 27.7% (#9126).
- The d2048 rung stopped at 81%. Beyond 80% we extend it along its own 60–80% linear trend, plus the deviation that each completed GB200 rung (d768, d1024, d1536) showed from *its* 60–80% trend.
- That gives three profiles with equal weight. For the 15-subset macro they are about 0 at 85–95% and +0.001 to +0.003 at 100%. v1 instead added U[0.003, 0.006] at every point beyond 80%.

**Uncertainty we sample over (60,000 draws):**
- ladder;
- compute convention: with or without lm_head FLOPs, 0.5 each;
- E ~ U[1.3, 1.7] without lm_head, U[1.5, 1.9] with it;
- d2048 profile;
- estimation error of a and b;
- κ, ε, β and η.

**Extrapolation distance.** The hero's compute is 337× the largest GB200 rung and 1,890× the largest H100 rung, while the backtests reach 6.5–166×.
- **Backtest errors drift pessimistic with distance, but the evidence is weak.**
  - The mean error is −0.0005 at 6.5–8×, +0.0031 at 52× and +0.0069 for the 67B at 166×.
  - A linear fit in log10 distance gives +0.0046 per decade (SE 0.0024, clustered by case with a small-sample correction). Fitting the 9 case means instead gives the same slope with SE 0.0034, t = 1.35. Without the 67B the slope is +0.0034 (case-mean t = 0.66).
  - The two 52× cases share their training rungs (H100 d512 + d768), and their targets also appear among the 6.5–8× cases.
  - The 67B differs from the ladder cases in method, target, eval length (8K) and endpoint (a mid-schedule point, not the end of a decay).
- **The drift tracks the floor E.** It grows with E and is larger when lm_head FLOPs are counted. For the 15-subset macro at 52×, the mean error is +0.0003 at E = 1.3 without lm_head and +0.0073 at E = 1.9 with it. This fits the 67B backtest, where E at the low end of our priors fit best. β is nevertheless applied the same way to every E and convention draw.
- **Checks within the hero agree only partly.** Without β, the two full ladders give the same primary median (2.0386), even though they extrapolate 337× and 1,890×. Dropping rungs to extrapolate further gives the 15-subset centers below. The H100 ladder rises by about +0.003 per decade, while the GB200 ladder does not.

  | Ladder (rungs) | Extrapolation | 15-subset center |
  |---|---|---|
  | GB200 (d768–d2048) | 337× | 2.0512 |
  | GB200 (d768–d1536) | 1,890× | 2.0511 |
  | GB200 (d768, d1024) | 15,126× | 2.0433 |
  | H100 (d512–d1536) | 1,890× | 2.0514 |
  | H100 (d512–d1024) | 15,126× | 2.0542 |
  | H100 (d512, d768) | 98,536× | 2.0566 |

Because the trend is suggestive but not significant, we hedge rather than apply it in full: β ~ U[0, b(d)]. One end assumes no distance bias; the other applies the full backtest trend, which b(d) extrapolates 0.3–1.1 decades beyond the 67B. The allowance lowers the median by 0.004. Applying none of it gives 2.039; applying all of it gives 2.031.

**PTB.** The 16-subset macro is forecast as `macro15 + D/16`, where D = PTB − macro15 (an exact identity, checked on the ladder rungs).
- **Current level:** a linear fit to the 35 clean evals with p ≥ 0.299 puts D at −0.123 now, with scatter SD 0.042.
  - The fit leaves out the three evals around the first read (206,999–212,999).
  - Its residuals have lag-1 autocorrelation 0.50. We therefore widen the level's standard error from 0.015 (ordinary least squares) to 0.025, a factor of √((1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ)).
- **Remaining change:** taken from 10 ladder rungs (GB200, H100 new mix and H100 old mix): mean −0.048, SD 0.016, widened to 0.02.
- **Did the first exposure leave a lasting shift? Unclear.**
  - The 5 evals since average −0.149. The line fitted to the 30 clean evals before the exposure is flat at about −0.088.
  - But that earlier series is noisy (residual SD 0.042, lag-1 autocorrelation 0.47). The four evals at steps 191,999–200,999 also averaged −0.150.

## 5. Limitations
- **Extrapolation distance.** The hero extrapolates 337–1,890× beyond the largest rungs, while the backtests reach 166×. The distance trend is not significant at the case level and is extrapolated beyond its data; the uniform hedge is a judgment.
- **Few cases.** There are 9 backtest cases, and several share a target rung. The size of ε is therefore itself uncertain, which is why ε has Student-t tails.
- **Judgment calls:** the 10% tolerance that sets κ_max, the uniform form of the distance allowance, and the PTB allowance, which rests on a single earlier exposure. The sensitivity table shows each.
- **Uniform β:** β does not vary with E or the compute convention, although the backtests suggest the bias is concentrated in high-E and lm_head draws.
- **Anchor regression:** the regression for a and b uses ordinary least squares and ignores autocorrelation. Only the PTB level's standard error is widened for it.
- **Context switch:** its effects on 4K-packed evals are outside the model and are handled by the conditions.
- **Revision timing:** v2 was written after v1 was published, but before any newer hero eval existed.
  - Changes 1–4 come from backtests on the ladders and the 67B.
  - Change 5 comes from the hero's own PTB evals, all of which were already in v1's snapshot, and from the exposure steps in #9874.
  - #9874's step mapping is the team's; we have not checked it independently.

## 6. Changes from v1
1. **Drift prior κ:** U[0, 1] → U[0, 0.2].
   - Why: in backtests of the same estimator, the error is smallest near κ = 0.15 and grows quickly beyond that (RMS 0.0127 at κ = 0.5, 0.0284 at κ = 1). v1's prior was a judgment.
   - Effect: median −0.003; most of the narrower interval.
2. **d2048 beyond 80%:** constant +U[0.003, 0.006] → empirical profiles from the completed GB200 rungs.
   - Why: those rungs show essentially no deviation at 85–95%, so v1 over-corrected.
   - Effect: −0.003.
3. **Method error:**
   - The backtest now scores the same estimator as the forecast; v1 scored it with κ = 0 but forecast with κ ~ U[0, 1].
   - Added two 52× pseudo-heroes, and the 67B now enters the error pool for the 15-subset target.
   - ε is Student-t with ν = 8 instead of Normal.
   - Effect: ε is slightly wider (SD 0.0057 → 0.0062) with heavier tails; the median does not change.
4. **Distance-bias allowance (new):** β ~ U[0, b(d)], from the backtest error trend in log distance.
   - Why: v1 treated the method error as independent of distance, but the backtests drift pessimistic as distance grows, though not significantly.
   - Effect: −0.004.
5. **PTB:**
   - The allowance U[−0.06, 0], which v1 phased in linearly, is now r2 ~ U[−0.06, 0], applied from the second exposure at step 362,280.
   - The current level's standard error is widened for autocorrelation (0.015 → 0.025).
   - Why: #9874 dates the second exposure, and the hero's PTB gap is autocorrelated.
   - Effect: none on the end-of-run median. Trajectory points before step 362,280, and shortened runs that end before it, no longer carry the allowance.
6. **Validation:**
   - The primary composite target is now backtested and calibrated itself; in v1 only the 15-subset and the direct 16-subset variants were.
   - Each leave-one-out fold now also re-selects κ_max and the distance trend.
   - The 67B branch now includes eval noise.
7. **Shortened-horizon table:** a run that completes its decay early now gets the full remaining change in D. v1 scaled it by the remaining progress, which made its 80% entry about 0.001 too high.
8. **Code, no numerical effect on this data:**
   - Duplicate steps across runs of the lineage now take the most recent run (v1 took the earliest).
   - Trajectory files now use the step convention in Section 2, with fractions to six decimals.
9. **Scoring rules, made more precise:**
   - step-to-fraction convention and interpolation;
   - the rollback rule;
   - lengthened horizons and other schedule changes;
   - the PTB-exposure rule;
   - the quantile score at trajectory points.

## 7. Errata for the v1 document
The v1 forecast table matched its frozen results. These statements in the text did not:
- "an 80% interval of ±0.017": the interval was asymmetric, −0.021 / +0.013 around the median.
- The trajectory table at 80% progress: the lower 80% bound was 2.079, not 2.080.
- "fitted on all evals after the data swap (steps 116,999–227,999, 38 evals)": the fit uses p ≥ 0.299; the two post-swap evals before that are excluded.
- "In our analysis at 57.7% of training … span about 0.2 … 0.086–0.109": these numbers came from an exploratory run on an earlier snapshot and are not in the published results.
- "PTB alone has eval-to-eval SD ≈ 0.066": that figure included the three contaminated evals; without them it is about 0.034.
- "that variant gives a median of 2.042": it was 2.04148, which rounds to 2.041.
- "all 20 per-5% points agree to within 0.0005": the largest difference was 0.00054.
- "(… plus the 67B) has an RMS of 0.006 for the 15-subset macro": the 67B entered only the 16-subset figure.
- "80% intervals cover … 11 of 14 (16-subset)": this was the direct 16-subset variant, not the primary composite. The same applies to the "79–83%" in the v1 README.
- "ending at 80% with a completed decay gives a median of 2.055": about 0.001 too high from the ΔD scaling (see change 7).
- "The largest pseudo-hero has 1.2B active parameters": the largest pseudo-hero target is d1536, about 481M active. The 1.2B rung (d2048) was only used as a training rung.
- `results/hero_actual.csv`, `results/step2_*` and `results/step3/` were produced from an earlier snapshot (data through step 224,999), not the frozen one.
- `code/check_snapshot.py` needs the full snapshot, which is not redistributed, so it fails on the published data.

# Addendum, 2026-10-09: the lm_head finding under the Oct 3 refit's exact setting

This addendum does not change the frozen forecast. It makes one finding in [#9977](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9977) more precise.

**Why.** The issue and Section 4 of `preregistration_v2.md` quote the lm_head effect on the H100 d768–d1536 rungs. - Rungs: H100 ladder, d512–d1536, old and new mixes.
- Progress points: the 15 points from 30% to 100%.
- Fit: one floor shared by all fits, chosen by least squares in loss space.
